content: I have a project that has some parts of proofs repeated two or three times with slight variations and I feel like there should be a more efficient way to write the proofs with less repetition, but a lot of times when I try to have a lemma or a have expression that depends on the different variables that change in the different cases it gets longer than the original way of writing each case. I was wondering if you have some tips for better organization of the code to reduce repetitions in a smart way.
It's not always easy, but usually try to have really a lot of small lemmas, as general as possible. If you have a short example we can maybe help more

Riccardo Brasca said:

It's not always easy, but usually try to have really a lot of small lemmas, as general as possible. If you have a short example we can maybe help more

O.k, thanks, I'll try so see what I can do. I would've liked to sent here the example, but it's probably too long.

I tried to create a very simplified example:

import Mathlib

theorem ex : Continuous (fun t ↦ ![Real.cos t, Real.sin t]) := by
  rw [continuous_pi_iff]
  intro i
  fin_cases i
  · simp
    exact Real.continuous_cos
  · simp
    exact Real.continuous_sin

Just to get some idea for better code writing, how would you write this proof, without having to repeat the two cases, slightly differently? And maybe image that we had a longer more complicated proof that is almost identical in both cases, except that in one case you are using different properties of Real.cos and in the second case you use the corresponding different properties of Real.sin.
Hmm, I am not super familiar with this part of the library, but I think your are suffering because that may not be the idiomatic way of defining the function.

import Mathlib

theorem ex : Continuous (fun t ↦ ![Real.cos t, Real.sin t]) := by
  rw [continuous_pi_iff]
  intro i
  fin_cases i <;> simp <;> fun_prop

is already shorter, but I am expecting fun_prop to be able to do it at once.

import Mathlib

theorem ex : Continuous (fun t ↦ (Real.cos t, Real.sin t)) := by
  fun_prop

And if I wanted this function to be to Euclidean space, i.e.: fun t => !₂[Real.cos t, Real.sin t]?
And more generally if the property we prove for each coordinate is more complicated and takes a few lines to prove?

I've never worked with euclidean spaces in mathlib so I don't know.

Concerning the coordinates (but this can help everywhere else), I would say that the trick is to teach fun_prop to use the relevant lemmas.

Concerning the coordinates (but this can help everywhere else), I would say that the trick is to teach fun_prop to use the relevant lemmas.

How can you teach it to use the relevant lemmas?
You can add a @[fun_prop] attribute to a lemma.

Michael Rothgang said:

You can add a @[fun_prop] attribute to a lemma.

Even if this lemma wasn't written by me?
There are probably a number of lemmas that could be tagged fun_prop, but are not. Changing that happens not rarely.
Do you mean, I can edit the Mathlib files where these lemmas are, and that's normal?
Yes, that is fine!

module
public import Mathlib

open Matrix

@[fun_prop]
lemma continuous_vecCons {α n} [TopologicalSpace α] :
    Continuous (fun p : α × (Fin n → α) ↦ vecCons p.1 p.2) := by
  rw [continuous_pi_iff]
  rintro (_ | _) <;> simp <;> fun_prop


theorem ex : Continuous (fun t ↦ ![Real.cos t, Real.sin t]) := by
  fun_prop

You can also experiment with a change without rebuilding the file, by doing attribute [fun_prop] my_fancy_lemma in your current file (as opposed to tagging my_fancy_lemma where it is defined and rebuilding a lot of files).
Yes exactly something like that. Note that you cal also do attribute [fun_prop] foo even after foo is defined.

Michael Rothgang said:

Yes, that is fine!

O.k, that's surprising, thanks!

This works the euclidean space for example

import Mathlib

open Matrix

attribute [fun_prop] Continuous.comp'

@[fun_prop]
lemma continuous_vecCons {α n} [TopologicalSpace α] :
    Continuous (fun p : α × (Fin n → α) ↦ vecCons p.1 p.2) := by
  rw [continuous_pi_iff]
  rintro (_ | _) <;> simp <;> fun_prop

theorem ex : Continuous (fun t => !₂[Real.cos t, Real.sin t]) := by
  fun_prop
Oh well, attribute [fun_prop] Continuous.comp' is not even needed. Anyway this is the idea.
Thank you very much to everyone, I'll try to learn this and apply it to my code.

By the way, are there any reasons not to add the fun_prop attribute to lemmas about function properties?

And another question: Suppose I have a proof which is like 5 lines long and works as is for all the cases (goals) is there a more elegant way to apply it to all the goals other than using 5 times <;>?
Do you know about the all_goals combinator?
(The other standard option is "make these five lines a lemma". Most proofs in mathlib are really short, because we like factoring out reusable results when we see them.)

Michael Rothgang said:

Do you know about the all_goals combinator?

I read about it once, but never used it. How is it different from <;>?

all_goals take a block, i.e. an indented sequence of tactics. (Searching for all_goals in mathlib should show you some examples.) So, you can do

apply foo
all_goals
  simp
  grind

instead of apply foo <;> simp <;> grind. (Made up example, so ignore any silliness.)

You are looking for on_goal or pick_goal.
Do you know the tactic cheatsheet? That has a few more trick. swap and rotate_left come to mind.

here's another proof:

import Mathlib

theorem ex : Continuous (fun t ↦ ![Real.cos t, Real.sin t]) := by
  apply Continuous.finCons
  · continuity
  apply Continuous.finCons
  · continuity
  continuity
(As a rule of thumb, fun_prop is better than continuity when both work.)

For the purpose of learning ways of avoiding (manual) repetition, here is one ( same as Eric's ) with tactic combinators :

import Mathlib

theorem ex : Continuous (fun t ↦ ![Real.cos t, Real.sin t]) := by
   repeat first | apply Continuous.finCons ; fun_prop | fun_prop

Avoiding repeating fun_prop , but arguably similar repetition because of first :

theorem ex : Continuous (fun t ↦ ![Real.cos t, Real.sin t]) := by
   repeat first | first | apply Continuous.finCons | fun_prop
It would be great if someone could look at hooking up docs#Continuous.finCons (and a vecCons duplicate) with fun_prop
@Michael Rothgang, in your opinion should that have been written as continuous_finCons instead, in the style of @Riccardo Brasca's lemma?
I would have replaced continuity with fun_prop; that was all I meant. (I didn't think about the other trade-off yet.)

If I have several goals, I can use all_goals <a sequence of tactics> to perform a sequence of tactics on all the goals and then continue to solve what left of each goal separately (maybe using the \. notation), but what if I want to start with performing different tactics for the different goals and then use all_goals to perform a sequence of tactics on what's left of all the goals? How can this be done?
I think with on_goal on each goal or otherwise with something like swap
Mathlib may lint against it, I'm not sure

I don't understand how exactly we could use on_goal or swap in this situation, maybe I didn't explain my self clearly, so I tried to create a stupid example to demonstrate what I'm trying to ask:

import Mathlib

example {x y : ℝ} : (x < y → x+1 < y+1) ∧ (0 ≤ 5) := by
  constructor
  · intro h
    linarith
  · linarith

--What I would have liked to do (but get an error):
example {x y : ℝ} : (x < y → x+1 < y+1) ∧ (0 ≤ 5) := by
  constructor
  · intro h
  all_goals
    linarith

in this example we have two goals that both end with the same sequence of tactics (in this case it's only one tactic - linarith), but the first one also start with a different tactic. I would have liked to do something like in the second example: perform on the first goal the tactics that are unique to it (the intro h line) and then perform on both goals the common tactics that both end with (in this case only one tactic linarith). Obviously in this specific example there is probably a better way to prove this example altogether, but that's not the point, this artificial example only meant to demonstrate what I'm asking about.
